176.title: Legion (Mark 5:1–13)
176.hook: a man among the tombs, chained and screaming, meets Jesus on the shore
176.howItsDone: Many Christians pray by name for people who are suffering in mind or spirit, and churches offer pastoral care, and in some traditions prayers of deliverance, alongside medical and mental health care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a storm, a cushion and a great calm. Your line was why are you afraid? Did you ask a fear that question? Day one hundred seventy-six.

The boat that came through the storm lands on the far shore. This is the other side in every sense: Gentile country, where people keep pigs. And the first thing that meets Jesus as he steps out is a man running at him from a graveyard. He lives among the tombs. People have tried to chain him, hand and foot, and he snaps the chains. Night and day he cries out in the hills and hurts himself. No man could tame him, Mark says. By any measure the town has, he's too far gone. Today: Legion.
screen: `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE LAKE.` → `A MAN AMONG THE TOMBS.` → `CHAINS THAT WON'T HOLD.`

segments.voice: Mark tells it with every detail of the horror, and then the strangest turn. The man runs to Jesus and falls on his knees. The voice that comes out of him shouts, what have I to do with thee, Jesus, Son of the most high God? And Jesus asks a simple, human question. What's your name? In the old King James Bible the answer is chilling: "My name is Legion: for we are many." A legion was a unit of the Roman army. The word is Latin, carried into Mark's Greek. So the man has no name of his own anymore. Just a crowd, an army, inside him. Some readers hear an edge in that word too: in a land under Roman rule, a man possessed by a legion. The spirits beg to be sent into a large herd of pigs feeding on the hillside, and Jesus lets them. The herd, about two thousand, Mark says, rushes down the steep bank into the lake. It's a wild, unsettling scene, and Mark doesn't explain everything about it. What he's clear on is the man. Look at how far out he is: living among the dead, beside animals the law of Moses calls unclean, out of reach of chains and neighbors. And Jesus crossed a storm to get to him. Churches differ on how to speak about what troubled him: some read the story alongside illness of the mind, and others stress that it describes spiritual forces too. What the story itself shows is plain: a man nobody could reach, reached.
screen: `WHAT IS THY NAME?` · `MY NAME IS LEGION.` · `A HERD RUSHES INTO THE LAKE.` · `NOBODY IS BEYOND REACH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone living in torment. Settle, and breathe gently. Let one person come to mind who is struggling badly right now. Addiction, despair, illness of the mind, a life that feels like it's lived among the tombs. Maybe someone everyone else has given up on. Hold their real name, the one underneath the struggle. If you pray, you can pray for them by that name. If you don't, hold them in mind with as much care as you can. If that person is you, you're allowed to hold yourself the same way, and to reach out for help. The bell holds the time.
Legion. A Roman army unit, and the name a tormented man gives when he's lost his own: we are many.
Your line: no one is too far. Today, send one message to someone who's been out of reach, or who might think they are. Day one hundred seventy-six.

what a scholar hears: legion is a Latin army word in Greek, and some hear in it a jab at Roman power.

177.title: Go home and tell (Mark 5:14–20)
177.hook: the healed man wants to follow, but Jesus sends him home to tell his own people
177.howItsDone: Many Christians share their faith first with family and friends by telling what God has done in their own lives, a practice often called giving testimony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man among the tombs who called himself Legion, met and set free. Your line was no one is too far. Who did you reach toward? Day one hundred seventy-seven.

The pig keepers run. Of course they do. They race into town and out to the farms, telling everyone what happened on the shore. And people come out to see. Here's what they find. The man they'd chained, the one who screamed all night in the hills, is sitting quietly next to Jesus, dressed, calm, himself again. You'd expect a party. Instead, Mark says, they were afraid. And they ask Jesus to leave. Today the story turns to the healed man, and what he wants most, and what he's told to do instead. Today: go home and tell.
screen: `THE PIG KEEPERS RUN.` → `THE TOWN COMES OUT.` → `THEY ASK HIM TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, the town finds him "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid." Mark doesn't say exactly why. The herd is gone, and the people who saw it tell that part too. And a change this big can be frightening in itself. So they ask Jesus to go. As he's getting into the boat, the healed man begs to come too. You can understand it. This is the one person who didn't give up on him. Why would he stay here, among the people who chained him? But Jesus says no. "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee." It's a surprise in Mark. Remember the man with leprosy, back on day one hundred sixty-two? Jesus told him to tell no one. Over and over in Mark, he tells people to keep quiet. Here, in Gentile country, he says the opposite: go and tell. And the man does. "And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel." Decapolis means ten cities, a region of Greek-speaking towns. Notice the small shift. Jesus told him to tell what the Lord had done. He tells what Jesus had done. Some readers see in that shift a hint of who Jesus is. And some call this man an early messenger to the Gentiles, sent before any apostle. His mission field wasn't far away. It was home, among the people who knew him at his worst.
screen: `SITTING, CLOTHED, IN HIS RIGHT MIND.` · `LET ME COME WITH YOU.` · `GO HOME TO THY FRIENDS.` · `TEN CITIES HEARD IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone at home a good thing. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last month. What's one good thing that happened to you? A kindness someone did. A prayer that felt answered, if you pray. A day you got through that you weren't sure you would. Let it come back in detail. Now picture the people at home, or the people who knew you before. Choose one. Imagine telling them, simply, what happened and who helped. The bell holds the time.
Go home and tell. What Jesus told the healed man when he begged to follow: your mission is the people who knew you.
Your line: go home and tell. Today, tell one person at home one good thing that happened to you, and who was kind to you in it. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

178.title: The hem of his garment (Mark 5:21–34)
178.hook: a woman bleeding twelve years touches his cloak in the crowd; he stops to find her
178.howItsDone: Many Christians pray for the chronically ill with this story in mind, and some churches offer prayer for healing with the laying on of hands or anointing with oil, alongside medical care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a healed man begged to follow and was sent home instead. Your line was go home and tell. Who heard your good news? Day one hundred seventy-eight.

Back across the lake, a crowd is waiting. A synagogue leader named Jairus pushes through, falls at Jesus's feet and begs: my little daughter is dying. Come. And Jesus goes, with the whole crowd pressing around him, shoulder to shoulder, jostling down a narrow street. Everyone's in a hurry. A child's life is on the line. And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody is looking at. She's been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything she had on doctors, and she's only gotten worse. She doesn't want a scene. She just wants to reach one hand through. Today: the hem of his garment.
screen: `JAIRUS: MY DAUGHTER IS DYING.` → `A CRUSH OF PEOPLE.` → `ONE HAND REACHES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Mark slows down for her. In the old King James Bible she "had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse." That sentence could have been written today, about a long illness or a stack of medical bills. Under the purity laws of the time, a condition like hers also made ordinary life complicated: worship, touch, closeness. So she makes a quiet plan. "If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole." She touches his cloak from behind, and immediately the bleeding stops. She can feel it. And here's the turn. Jesus stops. In the middle of an emergency, with a dying child waiting, he stops and asks, "Who touched my clothes?" His disciples point out the obvious: look at this crowd, and you ask who touched you? But he keeps looking. And she comes forward, shaking, falls down, and tells him the whole truth. Then comes the first word he says to her: "Daughter." "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." He could have let her slip away healed. Instead he made sure she was seen, named family, and sent off in peace in front of everyone. And notice the numbers. She's been ill twelve years. Jairus's daughter, we'll learn tomorrow, is twelve years old. Mark wraps one story inside the other. One more small thing: the hem in today's title comes from Matthew and Luke. Mark just says his clothes.
screen: `MANY PHYSICIANS, NOTHING BETTERED.` · `IF I MAY TOUCH BUT HIS CLOTHES.` · `WHO TOUCHED MY CLOTHES?` · `DAUGHTER, GO IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for someone the crowd ignores. Settle, and breathe. Picture a crowd you move through every day. A hallway, a store, a street, a group chat. Now look for the person nobody's looking at. The one who's been tired for years. The one who reaches out quietly and then pulls back. Let one face come. Imagine stopping. Turning around. Asking a real question and waiting for the whole truth. If you pray, you can pray for that person now. The bell holds the time.
The hem of his garment. What a woman ill for twelve years reached for in the crowd, and the reason he stopped to find her.
screen: `THE HEM OF HIS GARMENT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: daughter, go in peace. Today, stop for one person you'd usually hurry past, and make sure they feel seen. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: Little girl, get up (Mark 5:35–43)
179.hook: Mark keeps his Aramaic words, talitha koum, and then: give her something to eat
179.howItsDone: Christians read this story as a sign of hope in the resurrection, and many congregations answer illness and grief with meals brought to the family's door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hem of his garment: a woman reached for his clothes in the crowd, and he stopped to find her. Your line was daughter, go in peace. Who did you stop for? Day one hundred seventy-nine.

While Jesus is still speaking to the woman, men come from Jairus's house. And they bring the news. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any more? Picture Jairus's face. He did everything right. He begged, he hurried, and the delay for someone else's healing cost him everything. Jesus overhears, turns to him, and says five words. Then he goes to the house anyway, where the mourners have already started wailing. And in that small room, Mark keeps Jesus's words in the language he said them in. Today's word: talitha koum.
screen: `YOUR DAUGHTER IS DEAD.` → `WHY TROUBLE HIM ANY MORE?` → `FIVE WORDS TO JAIRUS.`

segments.voice: The five words, in the old King James Bible: "Be not afraid, only believe." At the house, the crying is loud. Jesus says the child isn't dead but sleeping, and they laugh at him. So he sends everyone out except her mother and father and three disciples, Peter, James and John. Then, "he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Talitha koum. Mark wrote in Greek, but here he keeps the Aramaic words, and then translates them for his readers. Talitha is a tender word, something like little girl. Koum means get up. It's what you might say to a child on a school morning. No grand formula. Just her hand in his and, little girl, get up. And she does. She gets up and walks around, and Mark adds, for she was twelve years old. The same twelve years the woman in the crowd had suffered. Then two closing lines, and both are so human. He tells them to keep it quiet. And he "commanded that something should be given her to eat." The miracle ends with a snack. Christians read this as a sign of Jesus's power over death, and of the hope of resurrection. Some readers treasure the ending too: after the impossible thing, the practical one. A child who's been very sick needs food. Care doesn't stop at the miracle. It goes on to the kitchen.
screen: `BE NOT AFRAID, ONLY BELIEVE.` · `HE TOOK HER BY THE HAND.` · `TALITHA KOUM: LITTLE GIRL, GET UP.` · `GIVE HER SOMETHING TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone today. Settle, and breathe. Let yourself hear it: talitha koum, little girl, get up. Said to a child, gently, holding her hand. Now think of someone who needs to get up from something: an illness, a grief, a long bad season. Then ask the practical question Jesus asked. What do they need to eat? Is there a meal you could bring, a coffee you could buy, a snack you could share? Choose one. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you plan it. The bell holds the time.
Talitha koum. Aramaic for little girl, get up. Mark kept the sound of it, then translated it.
Your line: talitha koum. Today, help someone get up by doing the practical thing, and feed someone, even if it's only a snack. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

180.title: Without honor at home (Mark 6:1–6)
180.hook: his hometown asks, isn't this the carpenter? and he can do little there
180.howItsDone: Many Christians honor Jesus's years as a working craftsman, and Catholics keep a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1; churches often draw on this story when talking about faith at home and at work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small room, a small hand, and two Aramaic words: talitha koum, little girl, get up. Did you feed someone? Day one hundred eighty.

You know what it's like to go home for the holidays. You've changed. You've learned things, done things, maybe become someone new. And within an hour at the table, you're twelve again. Somebody brings up the time you broke the window. Your cousin still calls you by the old nickname. That's Jesus, today. He's healed crowds, calmed a storm, raised a child. And he walks back into Nazareth, the village he grew up in, and teaches in the synagogue on the sabbath. And the people who watched him grow up can't quite get past who he used to be. Today: without honor at home.
screen: `HOME FOR THE HOLIDAYS.` → `BACK TO NAZARETH.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO KNEW HIM.`

segments.voice: At first they're amazed. Where did he get all this? Then, in the old King James Bible, the questions turn: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" They name his brothers, James, Joses, Judas and Simon, and say his sisters are right here with us. "And they were offended at him." Mark is the only gospel that calls Jesus himself the carpenter. Matthew says the carpenter's son. The Greek word is tekton, a builder, someone who works with wood and maybe stone. Doors, roofs, plows, yokes. Jesus worked with his hands, probably for most of his adult life, in a village of a few hundred people where everyone knew the builder. That's exactly the problem. How can the man who might have fixed our door be a prophet? Jesus answers with a line that became a proverb: "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house." Then comes one of the most striking sentences in Mark: "he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk, and healed them." Could. Not would. Matthew, telling the same story, says he did not do many. And one more line: "he marvelled because of their unbelief." Usually the crowds marvel at him. Here he marvels at them. Early copyists seem to have found it uncomfortable too: some manuscripts of Mark change the question to the son of the carpenter. Many Christians read the scene as a sign of how much trust matters, and how familiarity can close a door. And many find it comforting that the Son of God had a hometown that didn't get him, and a trade, and calluses.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` · `TEKTON — A BUILDER WITH HIS HANDS.` · `A PROPHET, AT HOME.` · `HE COULD DO NO MIGHTY WORK THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be kind to someone you've known forever. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've known so long you've stopped really seeing them. A sibling. A parent. An old friend. A spouse. The coworker who's been there longer than the furniture. Notice the old label you carry for them. Then ask what might be true about them now that you've missed. Something they've learned, or carried, or become. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Without honor at home. Jesus in Nazareth, among the people who knew him as the carpenter, and couldn't see past it.
Your line: isn't this the carpenter? Today, do one kind thing for someone you've known forever, and let them be someone new to you. Day one hundred eighty.

181.title: Travel light (Mark 6:7–13)
181.hook: he sends them out two by two with a staff and no bag
181.howItsDone: Many churches send people out in pairs to visit and serve, and many anoint the sick with oil; Catholic and Orthodox Christians count the anointing of the sick among the sacraments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, without honor at home: Nazareth looked at Jesus and asked, isn't this the carpenter? Did you see someone old in a new way? Day one hundred eighty-one.

The charger, the spare charger, the just-in-case sweater, snacks, a book that won't get read. A suitcase can hold every disaster a person can imagine. Right after his own hometown turns him away, Jesus does something bold. He doesn't pull back. He multiplies. He sends the twelve out, in pairs, to the villages, to do what he's been doing. And before they go, he gives them a packing list. It's very short. Today: travel light.
screen: `THE JUST-IN-CASE SWEATER.` → `SENT OUT IN PAIRS.` → `A VERY SHORT PACKING LIST.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old King James Bible: "take nothing for their journey, save a staff only; no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse: But be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats." A staff, for walking. Sandals. One coat. That's it. A scrip was a traveler's bag for food. No bag means no stockpiling. They'll eat what they're given. Which means they have to be received. That's the point. Travelers without supplies depend on hospitality. Jesus tells them: when a house takes you in, stay there. Don't shop around for a better one. And if a place won't have you, shake the dust off your feet as you leave, as a testimony against them, and move on. Why two by two? Mark doesn't say. Nobody walks alone that way, and the law of Moses says a matter is settled by two witnesses. So they go, and Mark says they preached that people should turn around and start again, drove out demons, and "anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them." Later, the letter of James tells the sick to call the elders to anoint them with oil. Churches still do it, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians count it among the sacraments. One more detail: Mark lets them take a staff. Matthew and Luke say, not even a staff. Readers explain the difference in different ways. Either way, the list is short on purpose. Less in the bag means more need for each other, and more room for trust.
screen: `A STAFF, SANDALS, ONE COAT.` · `NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.` · `STAY WHERE YOU'RE WELCOMED.` · `ANOINTED WITH OIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one thing out of your bag. Settle, and breathe. Picture your bag, backpack, purse, or pockets. What do you carry every day just in case? Then go deeper: what else are you carrying? A worry you pack every morning. A grudge. A plan B for a plan B. Choose one thing, one object or one weight, that you could leave behind today. Picture setting it down. If you pray, you can hand it to God. After the bell, actually take something out. The bell holds the time.
Travel light. The twelve sent out in pairs with a staff, sandals and one coat, depending on welcome.
Your line: travel light. Today, carry one thing less, in your bag or in your head, and notice who you lean on instead. Day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: John's head (Mark 6:14–29)
182.hook: a drunken promise at a party and the death of the Baptist, told in flashback
182.howItsDone: Christians honor John the Baptist as a prophet who died for speaking the truth; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember his beheading with a feast on August 29.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve sent out in pairs with a staff and one coat. Your line was travel light. What did you leave behind? Day one hundred eighty-two. Twenty-six weeks.

While the twelve are out in the villages, the news reaches the palace. Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, hears what's being done in Jesus's name. People are guessing who Jesus is: Elijah come back, one of the old prophets. Herod has his own answer, and it's a guilty one. It's John, he says, the one I beheaded. He's risen. And then Mark stops the story and flashes back, to tell how John the Baptist died. Today: John's head.
screen: `NEWS REACHES THE PALACE.` → `IT'S JOHN, RISEN.` → `A FLASHBACK.`

segments.voice: Herod had married Herodias, who had been married to his brother. John told him to his face that it wasn't lawful. So Herod had him chained in prison. But here's the twist Mark gives us: Herod was fascinated by John. He feared him, knew he was a good and holy man, and listened to him gladly, even though it left him troubled. Then comes Herod's birthday. A banquet for the officials, the officers, the leading men of Galilee. The daughter of Herodias dances, and it pleases everyone. And Herod, in front of all his guests, makes an open-ended promise: ask for anything. Then he swears it, in the old King James Bible: "Whatsoever thou shalt ask of me, I will give it thee, unto the half of my kingdom." The girl goes out to her mother. What should I ask? And the answer comes back: the head of John the Baptist. On a platter, she adds. Now watch Herod. "And the king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her." He doesn't want to. He does it anyway, because backing down in front of the room would cost him face. A soldier goes to the prison. It's done. John's disciples come for the body and bury him. In the King James text, Mark never names the girl. The name Salome comes from the historian Josephus, who lists Herodias's daughter but doesn't tell this story. Mark doesn't say Herod was drunk either, only that it was a feast. But the scene has the feel of it: a big promise, made to impress, and one man too proud to take it back. That closes a week. Legion. Go home and tell. The hem of his garment. Talitha koum. The carpenter. Travel light. And John's head.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one promise that matters. Settle, and breathe. Think of the promises you've made lately. Big ones and tiny ones. I'll call you back. I'll be there. I'll fix it this weekend. Notice any you made to look good, or to end a conversation. Now choose one promise that really matters to someone, and that you've let slide. Picture keeping it. If you pray, you can ask for help to keep your word. If a promise was careless, it's all right to admit it and make a better one. The bell holds the time.
